source.title: Enhance Diffusion to Improve Robust Generalization
source.authors: Jianhui Sun; Sanchit Sinha; Aidong Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, though some equations and table formatting are flattened or corrupted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of training hyperparameters and a gradient-noise manipulation on robust generalization using different measures and an adversarial-training setting.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own experiments on adversarial test accuracy and train/test accuracy curves. The cited findings about ordinary large-batch training and other prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-rate and gradient-noise effects on adversarial robustness, which no listed version names. Batch size remains 128: the paper derives a batch-size prediction but does not compare large and small batches or test recipe adaptations as V5 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors derive a robust-generalization bound under local quadratic and Gaussian-noise assumptions, predict benefits from increasing the learning-rate/batch-size ratio, and report that DEAT improves PGD-10 robust test accuracy with little additional cost. Empirical validation varies learning rate and training method, not batch size.
record.recipe_differences: Studies adversarially robust generalization under PGD adversarial training and introduces DEAT; the claim versions concern natural-label generalization under standard training.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate settings change adversarial test accuracy; the text reports a positive relationship. DEAT improvement is reported across model architectures and learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard-trained models have higher standard test accuracy than adversarially trained models have robust test accuracy on CIFAR-10. This comparison alone does not establish the size of either training–test gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard and adversarial training yield substantially different test accuracies under their respective evaluation conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch size 128, robust test accuracy correlates positively with learning rate across the tested architectures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within the tested CIFAR-10 PGD-AT learning-rate range, larger learning rates are associated with higher PGD-10 robust test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: DEAT improves robust test accuracy over PGD-AT across tested architectures and learning rates; training curves show improvement despite worse training performance, explicitly discussed for ResNet and SENet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Manipulating gradient noise with DEAT can improve robust generalization in the tested CIFAR-10 adversarial-training settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 29th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD ’23)
record.problems: Experiments focus on CIFAR-10 robust accuracy under PGD-10, not the natural-label generalization versions. Most results report robust test accuracy rather than the actual train/test gap. The paper reports averages of 3 runs, but uncertainty is not shown for the main accuracy table. Table 2 formatting in the supplied text is flattened and partly difficult to assign.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows retained. The paper cites related large-batch/generalization findings, which are prior work and not its own results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets, workload thresholds, and adaptations that recover held-out performance. Neither the fixed-batch learning-rate sweep nor the theoretical bound tests these comparisons.
Dropout comparisons, small-data regimes, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its correlation with measured generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The paper's statement that its theory also applies to ordinary training is not an empirical batch-size comparison. Its introduction mentions non-adversarial DEAT improvements, but the supplied text provides no corresponding experiment.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation point.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and their tuning.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the standard training/test gap.

rows.subject: VGG
rows.operation_detail: Compared standard training (non-adversarial) with PGD adversarial training over epochs.
rows.value: Robust test accuracy is far from standard test accuracy; robust generalization gap is described as significant and much larger than normal training.
rows.note: The paper describes the gap qualitatively; this is adversarial robustness, outside the natural-label generalization versions.
rows.check: Figure 2 compares standard and robust test accuracy; that difference alone does not measure a training–test generalization gap or any listed version.
